meetings.title: Durham City Council April 6, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council convened on April 6, 2026, hearing ceremonial proclamations and extensive public comment regarding infrastructure, traffic, and flooding. The primary agenda item was the Preserve at Trinity (Sunhouse Realty) rezoning and utility extension request near the Eno River watershed. After robust debate on environmental constraints, traffic impacts, and housing affordability, the council approved the utility extension agreement and rezoning ordinance in 4-3 split votes, along with unanimously approving the consistency statement and excusing the mayor from an upcoming work session.

agenda_items.title: Opening, Moment of Silence, Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the meeting to order, followed by the Pledge of Allegiance led by Council Member Reese and a roll call establishing a full quorum of council members.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Items and Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Proclamations were presented recognizing National Community Development Week, Fair Housing Month, Black Maternal Health Week, and Realtors Week, with remarks from city staff and community partner representatives.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members shared announcements including appreciation for retiring Audit Services Director Dr. Germaine Brewington, opening night of the Durham Bulls baseball season, and an update on the legislative committee's meeting with state lobbyists Checkmate Government Relations regarding local revenue and transit funding.

agenda_items.title: Preserve at Trinity Rezoning & Utility Extension Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and consideration of a rezoning and utility extension agreement for Sunhouse Realty LLC (Preserve at Trinity), involving approximately 40 acres of residential suburban land, environmental protections, conservation easements, and affordable housing proffers. Extensive public comment and council debate focused on traffic impacts at North Roxboro and Infinity Road, Eno River watershed protection, stormwater management, public school funding contributions, and density compatibility.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed, 4-3, with dissenting votes from Council Members Baker, Burris, and Cook.

agenda_items.title: Excuse Mayor from Work Session on April 9, 2026
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered and approved excusing Mayor Leonardo Williams from the upcoming work session scheduled for Thursday, April 9, 2026.

votes.item_title: Utility Extension Agreement with Sunhouse Realty LLC
votes.discussion_detail: The City Council considered authorizing a utility extension agreement with Sunhouse Realty LLC. Council members debated the developer's scale and offers compared to community concerns regarding traffic and flooding impacts. Discussion touched on local versus state and federal funding burdens and potential contributions to the Durham Public Schools Foundation. The motion passed by a 4-3 vote, with Council Members Baker, Burris, and Cook voting in opposition.

votes.item_title: Ordinance Amending UDO for Preserve at Trinity Rezoning
votes.discussion_detail: The City Council considered an ordinance to amend the unified development ordinance by removing property from residential suburban 20 Eno Watershed Overlay District B and establishing it as planned development residential 6.185 office and institutional with a development plan. Council discussion regarding development pressures, infrastructure impacts, and community feedback preceded the vote. The motion passed 4-3, with Council Members Baker, Burris, and Cook voting no.

votes.item_title: Consistency Statement for Preserve at Trinity Rezoning (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.discussion_detail: The City Council considered adopting the required consistency statement under North Carolina General Statute Section 160D-605 regarding the Preserve at Trinity rezoning. Following the previous zoning and utility extension discussions, the consistency statement was presented for formal adoption. The motion passed unanimously (7-0).

votes.item_title: Excuse Mayor from Work Session on April 9, 2026
votes.discussion_detail: The City Council considered a procedural motion to excuse the mayor from the upcoming work session scheduled for Thursday, April 9, 2026. The mayor noted the need to be absent and requested facilitation of the motion. The motion was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously (7-0).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council April 6, 2026
disagreements.issue: Preserve at Trinity (Sunhouse Realty) Rezoning & Utility Extension
disagreements.summary: Debate over whether to approve rezoning and utility extension for a multi-family/townhome and office-institutional development near Infinity Road and the Eno River watershed, balancing housing need against environmental, traffic, and flood risks.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning, utility extension, and consistency statement.
side_a_arguments: The project is consistent with the comprehensive plan and place type map for transit opportunity areas.
Provides alternative housing types and increased affordability (8% AMI units, improved from 5%) by a local small business developer.

Includes significant environmental proffers (conservation easement for floodplain and stream, 100% native trees in OID, stormwater peak flow mitigation) and increased school donations ($1,000 per student).
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning and utility extension project.
side_b_arguments: Severe concerns regarding increased traffic congestion on North Roxboro and Infinity Road, compounded by unfunded state intersection improvements (STIP U-5516).
Environmental and watershed risks including proximity to the Eno River critical area, steep slopes, historical flooding in the area, and potential runoff impacts.
Insufficient affordable housing contribution relative to community need and potential displacement pressures.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 4-3 on the utility extension agreement and UDO amendment ordinance; passed unanimously on the consistency statement.

development_cases.location: 4840 Topgolf Way (adjacent to Page Road and I-40)
development_cases.scale: 1 parcel totaling 2.85 acres (part of ~50-acre Topgolf assemblage); maximum 4,000 sq ft conditioned interior space
development_cases.zoning_change: IP (Industrial Park, Major Transportation Corridor I-40 Overlay) to CG(D) (Commercial General with Textual Development Plan, Major Transportation Corridor I-40 Overlay)

proffers.environmental_tree: Maximum 50% impervious surface (exceeding UDO requirements); 100% native plant species; meeting 10% tree cover requirement on this parcel
proffers.transit_infrastructure: No direct vehicle access onto Page Road; 10-ft shared-use bike and pedestrian pathway adjacent to Page Road
other_proffers: Maximum 4,000 sq ft of conditioned interior space
Prohibited uses: electronic gaming operations, indoor firing ranges, payday lenders, living facilities, and educational facilities

development_cases.location: 301 and 401 Infinity Road (east of North Roxboro Street)
development_cases.scale: 2 parcels totaling approximately 18 acres; up to 90 multi-family/townhouse units and up to 5,000 sq ft of non-residential (office/institutional) uses
development_cases.zoning_change: RS-20 (Eno Watershed Overlay District B) to PDR 6.185 and OI(D) (Eno Watershed Overlay District B)

proffers.dps_cash: $1,000 per student (increased on the floor from $600/student / $15,000 total)
proffers.affordable_housing: 8% income-restricted units at 80% AMI for 30 years with 2 or more bedrooms (increased on the floor from 5%)
proffers.environmental_tree: 25% tree coverage (5% above UDO minimum); 100-ft stream buffer; 50% of open space containing environmentally sensitive areas; permanent conservation easement offered for floodplain and Recreation & Open Space area; existing floodplains and wetlands undisturbed except for single access/utility crossing; 100% native trees in both PDR and OI(D) districts (OI increased from 75% to 100% on the floor); stormwater control measure ensuring post-development peak flow does not exceed pre-development peak flow for the 100-year storm event at the Infinity Road culvert inlet
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-ft multi-use path along Infinity Road; pedestrian crosswalk with safe-crossing accommodations at Windermere Drive across Infinity Road to River Forest Park and Mountains-to-Sea Trail (subject to DOT); public street stub-outs to north and west
other_proffers: Variation in residential building appearance
Active open space

member_justifications.stance_summary: Presses the applicant on flooding, affordability, native species, and school contributions, securing on-the-floor commitments for 100-year storm peak-flow control at the Infinity Road culvert, increasing affordable units from 5% to 8%, and 100% native plantings in PDR. Praises the permanent conservation easement with DOST, the BPAC crosswalk to River Forest Park and the Mountains-to-Sea Trail, and the transit-opportunity infill location, while urging higher DPS contributions in future cases.
member_justifications.key_quote: I do want to acknowledge the partnership with DOST, that committee's work on this, and the acceptance of the recommendation of the permanent conservation easement, something I don't believe we've seen before.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Notes that the forested site already performs vital ecological, habitat, and stormwater filtration functions, so any development replacing it must truly make Durham better and advance the Comprehensive Plan. Argues this parcel lies on the far eastern edge of the Transit Opportunity Area farthest from actual transit on Roxboro Road, lacks cohesive planning across irregular parcels, and urges denial or continuance.
member_justifications.key_quote: If we are going to tear down something that is already valuable, whether it's forest or anything else, are we replacing it with something that makes Durham better? For me, this case does not reach that point.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Cites severe existing traffic backups and multi-cycle light delays along Infinity and North Roxboro with no state budget or NCDOT fix in sight as a quality-of-life barrier. Rejects 8% at 80% AMI (roughly seven units) as insufficient and warns against putting buyers at risk in an area adjacent to past flooding where insurance could become unattainable.
member_justifications.key_quote: I have not been moved based on the environmental concerns and also the lack of affordable housing... considering what's happening in our community right now, like seven units at this point for 80% does not move me.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Secures an increase from 75% to 100% native trees in the OI(D) parcel and confirms only one floodplain driveway crossing is planned. Concludes that for a small 90-unit site, the added 8% affordability, 100-year stormwater treatment, DOST conservation easement, and BPAC crosswalk/multi-use path commitments thread the needle and help meet projected regional growth.
member_justifications.key_quote: I think there's no perfect case. I think you've done a lot to really work with the community, with the council here to sort of thread the needle on this one.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Values that the applicant is a local Durham small business owner rather than a national builder and emphasizes the site is an infill parcel within city limits and a Transit Opportunity Area where by-right development would yield zero affordable housing or conservation easements. Also notes the resulting contiguous sidewalks and stormwater controls improve on existing conditions and asks for better tracking of DPS proffers.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is at the end of the day an infill project... All of the things that are being proffered currently would not necessarily have to be proffered.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports the small local developer and emphasizes Durham's need for housing at all income levels and types to support the tax base and close the housing gap. Argues the Comprehensive Plan was built with broad community input and this consistent infill project with engineered stormwater mitigation warrants approval.
member_justifications.key_quote: We went through all of that work to get the comprehensive plan consistent... when we have something that's consistent and it's still not good enough, everyone votes their conscience.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Expresses gratitude that the applicant raised the DPS donation to $1,000 per student and increased affordable for-sale units, but states her decision comes down to worsening climate-driven flooding. Citing flood damage to commercial buildings in Chapel Hill, she refuses to support development in or adjacent to a floodplain where future disaster risks are foreseeable.
member_justifications.key_quote: For me, it's going to come down to the question of the flooding... I don't want us to be looking back in 30 years and saying like, oh gosh, who chose to build in that flood plain?

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 19, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held a work session on March 19, 2026. The council discussed routine announcements, proclamations (declaring Cleaning Week), board and committee appointments, public comments regarding fire station vehicle break-ins and property conditions, a major review of options for the 505 West Chapel Hill Street site (including affordable housing and historic preservation of the Milton Small Building), and administrative updates to council agenda formatting. No formal roll-call votes or motions were recorded in this work session transcript.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members shared opening announcements, including Council Member Matt Kopac mentioning the Environmental Affairs Board letter on Duke Energy's carbon plan, Council Member Carl Rist highlighting March Madness and upcoming parks bond public meetings, and the Mayor Pro Tem discussing the reporting on Cesar Chavez and community survivors.

agenda_items.title: Proclamation for Cleaning Week (General Services Custodial Team)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams and the city council recognized the General Services Department custodial team and celebrated upcoming International Cleaning Week (cleaning week in Durham), highlighting the city's commitment to in-house cleaning staff with competitive wages and benefits rather than third-party outsourcing.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items, City Attorney Introduction, and Board & Committee Reports
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager reported no priority items for the City Manager's Office. City Attorney reported no priority items and introduced a new paralegal, Maryann Frati, focusing on affordable housing and real estate. City Clerk reported board and committee appointments (Daniel W. Cole, Lena G. Tonkan, Nicholas Monton, Priesty Willis) and noted lack of consensus for the Human Relations Commission appointment.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment: Fire Station Vehicle Break-ins (Local 668)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Meredith Carter spoke on behalf of Local 668 (Professional Firefighters of Durham) regarding frequent personal vehicle break-ins at fire stations across the city (stations 1, 3, 4, 5, 9, 12, and 16). She requested secure fencing or mobile security at every station and city support for vehicle repairs.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment: Council Punctuality, St. Joseph Historical Foundation, and Blighted Properties
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson expressed concern about council members and the mayor arriving late to work sessions, requested an itemized budget report regarding St. Joseph Historical Foundation and the $10M fund, and reported run-down properties on Ridgeway Avenue, Austin Avenue, and Fayetteville Street.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment: Land Development Code (LDC), Infill Standards, and Zoning Inequities
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Scott Harmon, architect and developer with Center Studio, spoke about historical zoning patterns, neighborhood character, minimum lot sizes, and how current infill standards in the Land Development Code (LDC) perpetuate systemic inequities in housing and land use.

agenda_items.title: 505 West Chapel Hill Street Site Redevelopment & Milton Small Building Preservation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council and staff discussed the 505 West Chapel Hill Street site redevelopment options, incorporating affordable housing, preserving the Milton Small Building with Preservation North Carolina, parking strategies, and coordination with financing partners. Extensive discussion took place on infill, tax credits, and future site activation.

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 16, 2026 (Full Audio)
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held its regular meeting on March 16, 2026, featuring several proclamations, public hearings on the upcoming FY 2027 budget and CIP, and votes on capital financing and zoning changes. The council debated and approved amendments to the Fayetteville Street Corridor Neighborhood Stabilization Partnership and grant agreement with Hataway Promise Community Development Corporation (removing St. Joseph's Historic Foundation as fiscal agent) in a 5-2 split vote. Additionally, the council unanimously approved a $136 million limited obligation bond resolution for capital projects, solid waste, and DPAC HVAC reimbursements, as well as a zoning map change for 1612 and 1562 Carpenter Fletcher Road.

agenda_items.title: Opening, Pledge of Allegiance & Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor pro tem opened the meeting, followed by a moment of silent meditation, the Pledge of Allegiance, and roll call confirming council members present.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations & Special Presentations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members read and presented proclamations for Bleeding Disorders Awareness Month, Durham Crop Hunger Walk, and International Women's History Month.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members shared community updates, recognized local sports achievements (Southern High School 7A state championship), and highlighted upcoming events and creek cleanups.

agenda_items.title: Fayetteville Street Corridor Stabilization & Hataway Promise CDC Grant Agreement Amendments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Extensive public comments and council debate regarding the first amendment to the ARPA/Revenue Recovery Subrecipient Grant Agreement and Fayetteville Street Corridor Neighborhood Stabilization Partnership with Hataway Promise CDC and St. Joseph's Historic Foundation. Discussion focused on fiscal oversight, transparency, community engagement, and progress tracking.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (5-2 on Item 12.1; unanimous on subsequent modifications and partnership amendments).

agenda_items.title: Limited Obligation Bonds Series 2026AB Installment Financing Contract
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City debt administrator presented the proposed limited obligation bond series 2026AB (not to exceed $136 million) to fund general capital projects, solid waste, and DPAC HVAC project costs. Public hearing was held with no speakers signed up.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed unanimously (Unanimous vote on installment financing contract resolution and legal document execution).

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change for 1612 and 1562 Carpenter Fletcher Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff and applicant presented a zoning map change request for 1612 and 1562 Carpenter Fletcher Road from Commercial General with textual development plan and office/institutional to Commercial General with textual development plan to expand permitted uses and commit to native landscaping species.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed unanimously (Unanimous vote on zoning map ordinance and consistency statement).

agenda_items.title: FY 2027 Budget & Capital Improvement Plan Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and Management Services director presented the public hearing to receive comments on the development of the FY 2027 budget and FY 2027-2032 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP).

votes.item_title: First Amendment to ARPA/Revenue Recovery Subrecipient Grant Agreement with Hataway Promise Community Development Corporation
votes.notes: Removes St. Joseph's Historic Foundation as fiscal agent and updates funding source up to $6,755,000.
votes.discussion_detail: This vote concerned the first amendment to the ARPA/Revenue Recovery Subrecipient Grant Agreement with Hataway Promise Community Development Corporation, involving a total amount not to exceed $6,755,000 to remove St. Joseph's Historic Foundation Inc. as fiscal agent and change the funding source. Council members debated major work products, reporting intervals, and community engagement, with Council Member Baker requesting reports at 6- to 12-month intervals until funds are fully expended. The motion passed 5-2, with Council Members Burris and Cook voting in opposition.

votes.item_title: Subsequent Modifications Authorization for Hataway Promise CDC Grant Agreement
votes.notes: Authorizes city manager to negotiate and make subsequent modifications up to $6,755,000.
votes.discussion_detail: This routine motion authorized the city manager to negotiate and make subsequent modifications to the amended grant agreement with Hataway Promise Community Development Corporation, provided that total grant funds do not exceed $6,755,000. The motion passed unanimously without recorded debate or opposition.

votes.item_title: Fayetteville Street Corridor Neighborhood Stabilization Partnership Agreement Amendment
votes.notes: First amendment involving Hataway Promise CDC, City of Durham, and Preserving Home Inc. to remove St. Joseph Historic Foundation as fiscal agent.
votes.discussion_detail: This vote authorized the first amendment to the agreement between Hataway Promise Community Development Corporation, the City of Durham, and Preserving Home Inc. (formerly Rebuilding Together of the Triangle Inc.) for the Fayetteville Street corridor neighborhood stabilization partnership implementation. The amendment removed St. Joseph Historic Foundation Inc. as fiscal agent. The motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Limited Obligation Bonds Series 2026AB Installment Financing Contract
votes.notes: Approving installment financing contract not to exceed $136 million for general capital, solid waste, and DPAC HVAC project costs.
votes.discussion_detail: This vote adopted a resolution approving an installment financing contract not to exceed $136 million along with an accompanying deed of trust, and provided for a public hearing concerning the contract to finance general capital, solid waste, and DPAC (Durham Arts) needs as presented by debt administrator John Reese. The motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Execution of Legal Documents for 2026AB Limited Obligation Bonds
votes.notes: Authorizing city manager/designate to execute associated legal documents.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the adoption of the financing contract, this vote authorized the city manager or his designate to execute other associated legal documents and make pre-execution changes consistent with the intent of the agenda item memo and existing document versions. The motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Zoning Map Change for 1612 and 1562 Carpenter Fletcher Road
votes.notes: Expanding permitted uses under Commercial General with textual development plan, including commitment to native species landscaping.
votes.discussion_detail: The council considered a zoning map change for 1612 and 1562 Carpenter Fletcher Road, amending the unified development ordinance to transition property out of commercial general with a textual development plan in office and institutional and establishing the same as commercial general with the textual development plan. Prior to the vote, discussion centered on landscaping commitments, with a council member asking for confirmation regarding the inclusion of native plant species. Staff confirmed they would work with the applicant the following day to secure official language committing to native species for future site landscaping changes and redevelopment. Following this clarification, the motion to adopt the ordinance was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously with zero nays.

votes.item_title: Consistency Statement for 1612 and 1562 Carpenter Fletcher Road Zoning Change
votes.discussion_detail: Following the approval of the zoning map change for 1612 and 1562 Carpenter Fletcher Road, the council considered the mandatory consistency statement as required by North Carolina General Statute section 160D-605. The motion to adopt the consistency statement was duly moved and seconded. The clerk opened and closed the vote, and the motion passed unanimously with no opposition.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 16, 2026 (Full Audio)
disagreements.issue: Fayetteville Street Corridor Stabilization Partnership & Hataway Promise CDC Grant Amendment
disagreements.summary: Debate over amending the Fayetteville Street corridor stabilization grant agreement to remove St. Joseph's Historic Foundation as fiscal agent and allocate funds up to $6,755,000 to Hataway Promise CDC.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support moving forward with the agreement and removing St. Joseph's Historic Foundation as fiscal agent.
side_a_arguments: Stated that Hataway Promise CDC has shown meaningful progress, that strict metrics and reporting intervals (six-month updates) are established, and that further delay would stall much-needed investment and restitution in a historically disinvested corridor.
disagreements.side_b_position: Voted against the agreement out of concern for financial oversight and accountability, while clarifying support for the corridor community.
side_b_arguments: Expressed caution regarding fiscal accountability and stewardship of public funds, questioning whether the expenditure would produce guaranteed benefits or become a lever against future investments.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 5-2, with Council Members Burris and Cook voting against.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 5, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held its work session on March 5, 2026, discussing critical infrastructure and community development items, including a wastewater collection system capacity overview highlighting capacity constraints in the Goose Creek basin and upcoming infrastructure projects, as well as an implementation update on the Fayetteville Street Corridor Neighborhood Stabilization Partnership involving Hayti Promise CDC. The council also heard extensive public comments on unpaved streets, traffic fatalities, park encampments, and gun violence, settled the meeting agenda, and voted to enter a closed session for attorney-client consultation and property damage claims.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Announcements, and Opening Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams called the work session to order, followed by a roll call and brief council announcements, including updates on joint city-county planning, environmental boards, and birthday wishes for Councilmember Kopac. Several councilmembers also raised community concerns regarding recent gun violence in Durham and conditions in correctional facilities.

agenda_items.title: Manager and Attorney Priorities & Closed Session Motion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager reviewed priority items, noting the withdrawal of one speaker under citizen matters. The City Attorney requested a closed session regarding pending federal litigation (Timothy Evans v. City of Durham et al.) and a property damage claim by Capital Associates, which was approved by unanimous voice vote.

agenda_items.title: DPAC Oversight Committee Mayoral Appointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk presented the mayoral appointment for the Durham Performing Arts Center (DPAC) Oversight Committee, recommending Scott F. Selig.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Reading and Item Pulls
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Mayor read the consent agenda items, and councilmembers discussed and pulled specific items for separate discussion and public comment (including items 10, 12, 13, and 14).

agenda_items.title: Citizen Matters / Public Comment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents spoke during citizen matters on various topics, including unpaved street and water infrastructure needs on Ottmar Drive, traffic safety and district attorney accountability regarding hit-and-run fatalities, park encampments at Oakwood Park, and gun violence prevention.

agenda_items.title: Wastewater Collection System Capacity Overview Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City staff delivered a comprehensive presentation on wastewater collection system capacity, focusing on the unexpected 100% capacity finding in the Goose Creek basin, ongoing outfall improvement projects, hydraulic modeling, and the issuance of Letters to Industry (LTIs) restricting development. Councilmembers questioned staff extensively regarding notice transparency and project timelines.

agenda_items.title: Fayetteville Street Corridor Project Implementation Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and representatives presented an update on the Fayetteville Street Corridor Neighborhood Stabilization Partnership Implementation, detailing the deployment of ARPA funds, historic preservation partnerships (Preservation Durham, Preserving Home Inc.), youth workforce training, and governance structures of the Hayti Promise CDC. Public speakers and councilmembers debated oversight, financial transparency, and community engagement.

agenda_items.title: Settle Agenda for Forthcoming Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager reviewed the items to be placed on the agenda for the forthcoming formal council meeting, and the council voted to settle the agenda.

votes.item_title: Closed Session (Timothy Evans v. City of Durham & Capital Associates property damage claim)
votes.discussion_detail: The City Attorney proposed a motion to resume into closed session post-agenda to discuss two legal matters: a federal district case in the Middle District (case 26-CV-181) involving Timothy Evans v. City of Durham, Irwin Baker, and James Edward Melvin II, as well as a property damage claim presented by Capital Associates and CPD Durham Center Investors. The motion was properly moved, seconded, and passed unanimously by voice vote with no opposition. Following the vote, the Clerk delivered board and committee reports, including the mayoral appointment of Scott F. Selig to the Durham Performing Arts Center Oversight Committee, followed by the reading of the consent agenda.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 5, 2026
disagreements.issue: Communication and notification transparency regarding wastewater capacity Letters to Industry in the Goose Creek basin
disagreements.summary: Councilmembers debated whether issuing letters to industry restricting development due to sewer capacity constraints without direct mailings to affected property owners was sufficient.
disagreements.side_a_position: Standard administrative practice via industry associations is sufficient.
side_a_arguments: LTIs were distributed through standard channels like the Home Builders Association and voluntary sign-up lists, consistent with past practice.
disagreements.side_b_position: Direct mailings or expanded property records outreach should be used to notify affected property owners.
side_b_arguments: Property owners were caught by surprise with halted development rights without direct notice or due process.
disagreements.resolution: Staff agreed to evaluate expanding notification methods and budgetary impacts for property-specific letters to industry in the future.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 5, 2026
disagreements.issue: Accountability, structure, and oversight of ARPA funding and community development for the Fayetteville Street Corridor (Hayti Promise CDC)
disagreements.summary: Councilmembers and community members debated the effectiveness, administrative hurdles, and oversight surrounding the Hayti Promise CDC and ARPA investments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Supportive of the bold ARPA investment and volunteer board efforts.
side_a_arguments: The initial ARPA allocation was a bold, necessary community-led risk and down payment addressing historical underinvestment in the corridor.
disagreements.side_b_position: Expressed caution and concern over administrative overhead, financial controls, and accountability.
side_b_arguments: High consultant expenditures, lack of established organizational capacity, and questions over financial transparency raised red flags.
disagreements.resolution: Discussion concluded with consensus on maintaining oversight, auditing future expenditures, and supporting ongoing corridor revitalization efforts while demanding accountability.

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 2, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council met on March 2, 2026, led by Mayor Leonardo Williams. The council recognized National Girl Scout Day, honored three GoDurham bus operators with Million Miler Club awards, and heard extensive public comments regarding gun violence, youth safety, and community investments. The council unanimously adopted the consent agenda (7-0) and later accepted the Fourth Quarter Crime Report (Item 12) also by a 7-0 vote. Council members also discussed upcoming difficult budget deliberations, including priorities such as fare-free buses and emergency home repairs.

agenda_items.title: Opening Roll Call, Pledge of Allegiance, and Girl Scouts & GoDurham Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The meeting opened with a roll call, a moment of silence, and the Pledge of Allegiance. Council presented ceremonial proclamations recognizing National Girl Scout Day and honoring three GoDurham bus operators inducted into the Million Miler Club for driving 1 million safe miles.

agenda_items.title: City Council Member Announcements & Regional Updates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members shared announcements regarding local business incubator openings, labor union events, community health fairs, condolences for fallen state trooper Steven Perry, concerns over ongoing conflicts in the Middle East, and upcoming budget retreat priorities and public hearings.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-11, 13-14)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager and Attorney provided brief administrative updates. Council reviewed and adopted the consent agenda, which included board appointments, financial reports, grant budget ordinances, contract awards, and interlocal agreements.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments on Community Safety and Crime
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Numerous community members, youth advocates, and student leaders spoke during public comment regarding community safety, youth violence, policing history, mental health support, and the need for greater investment in youth employment and community violence intervention initiatives.

agenda_items.title: 2025 Fourth Quarter Crime Report (Item 12)

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat: Day 2 - Friday, February 27, 2026 Part 1
meetings.executive_summary: Durham City Council held Day 2 of their budget retreat on Friday, February 27, 2026. City Manager Bo Ferguson briefed the council on severe fiscal constraints, warning that rising expenditures and constrained revenues will make achieving a balanced budget challenging and require difficult choices. Transportation Director Sean Egan also presented the transit and parking fund update, highlighting growing financial deficits and confirming that previous fund surplus projections have worsened.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams called the Durham City Council Budget Retreat (Day 2, Part 1) to order at 9:02 AM. Madam Clerk called the roll, establishing a quorum with Mayor Williams, Mayor Pro Tem Javiera Caballero, and Council Members Baker, Burus, Cook, Copac, and Rest present.

agenda_items.title: Day 2 Budget Retreat Overview and Opening Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and Management Services Director Christina Rearden outlined the full agenda for Day 2 of the budget retreat, highlighting morning sessions covering the City Manager's remarks, transit and parking fund updates, and Capital Improvement Program (CIP) discussions, followed by afternoon working sessions on city council budget requests, strategic plan priorities, and budget guidelines.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Budget Outlook and Opening Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Bo Ferguson delivered candid opening remarks expressing serious stress regarding the FY2026/2027 revenue and expenditure outlook, noting that revenue projections are underperforming while expenditure pressures are mounting. He emphasized that difficult choices and potential cuts will be necessary to achieve a balanced budget, and called on council members to practice rigorous and tactful honesty when prioritizing initiatives.

agenda_items.title: Transit Fund Financial Status and Revenue Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan and City Manager Bo Ferguson presented a critical financial update on the Transit Fund, recalling warnings from the previous year's budget retreat regarding fund balance depletion. They reported that the transit fund financial position has worsened due to underperforming revenues, presenting significant challenges for maintaining transit commitments and fare-free service.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat: Day 2 - Friday, February 27, 2026 - Part 3
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held Day 2 of their 2026 Budget Retreat (Part 3), discussing the 10-year Capital Improvement Program (CIP) model, debt capacity limits, and general fund revenue and expenditure balancing. Council members debated project prioritization frameworks, mayoral budget requests (such as funding for the 2029 World University Games and local economic activation), and options for closing the general fund budget gap without excessive property tax increases. The session served as a strategic working retreat to provide guidance to the city manager for upcoming budget recommendations, with no formal roll-call votes or binding legislative actions taken.

agenda_items.title: Capital Improvement Program (CIP) 10-Year Plan & Process Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented an overview of the 10-year Capital Improvement Program (CIP) budget process, highlighting the receipt of 70 general capital project requests totaling over $200 million for FY27. Council members discussed the need for long-term predictability, realism regarding construction cost overruns, and enhanced transparency for residents.

agenda_items.title: Finance Department & Debt Model Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director Tim Flora reviewed the city's debt model, fund cash flows, debt portfolio exceeding $1 billion ($614M utilities, $394M governmental), and key financial ratios (debt service as % of operating expense, debt per capita, and adherence to AAA credit rating targets).

agenda_items.title: Strategic Priority Buckets & Prioritization Framework Structure
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members debated the strategic priority buckets and prioritization framework structure, specifically addressing how to handle multiple overlapping goals, whether to split complex environmental/housing buckets, and how council-submitted initiatives interact with departmental requests.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Consensus reached via sticky-note voting and inclusion of additional categories without formal roll call tally.

agenda_items.title: General Fund Budget Gap Balancing & Revenue Options
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance staff presented preliminary general fund budget balancing options, including tax rate allocations (property tax, debt service, solid waste, dedicated housing, transit) and trade-offs between tax increases, employee pay-for-performance/step plans, and minimum livable wage adjustments.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat: Day 2 - Friday, February 27, 2026 - Part 3
disagreements.issue: Strategic Priority Buckets & Prioritization Framework Structure
disagreements.summary: Debate over whether to consolidate or separate categories in the strategic priority framework and how council member priorities fit alongside departmental submissions.
disagreements.side_a_position: Favorable to more granular category separation and tracking council priorities.
side_a_arguments: Argued for separating out specific categories (like resilience/environmental policies or distinct priority areas) and ensuring council member-specific initiatives and earmarks are clearly evaluated alongside departmental requests.
disagreements.side_b_position: Favorable to streamlined, focused priority buckets.
side_b_arguments: Emphasized that strategy is about choice, too many priorities dilute focus, and the ranking tool / sticky-note exercise provides clear directional signals to staff without needing overly fragmented goal categories.
disagreements.resolution: Council agreed to proceed with the structured priority ranking exercise while allowing individual council members to add specific items/priorities and use stickers for weighted preference signaling.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat: Day 2 - Friday, February 27, 2026 - Part 3
disagreements.issue: General Fund Budget Gap Balancing: Tax Increases vs. Compensation and Wage Adjustments
disagreements.summary: Discussion and debate over how to close the projected general fund budget gap and whether to raise property taxes or modify step plans, pay-for-performance, and part-time DMLW implementation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Reluctant to raise taxes; open to exploring targeted expenditure adjustments.
side_a_arguments: Strongly opposed raising property taxes due to resident tax fatigue and economic pressures, suggesting exploring reductions in pay-for-performance step percentages (e.g., from 5% down to 4%) or staging part-time DMLW implementations.
disagreements.side_b_position: Cautious about rolling back worker commitments while recognizing fiscal constraints.
side_b_arguments: Highlighted the importance of honoring commitments to city workers, maintaining living wage standards, and preserving employee benefits while acknowledging difficult fiscal trade-offs.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken; staff were directed to provide detailed scenarios and impact analyses on various revenue and expenditure balancing options for upcoming budget hearings.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat: Day 2 - Friday, February 27, 2026 Part 2
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council discussed transit financial forecasts, Go Durham Access paratransit contract cost pressures, and potential policy options for addressing transit fund deficits. The council also received a detailed presentation and feedback session on the Durham Cultural Roadmap, reviewing arts, culture, and civic infrastructure initiatives, as well as an update on federal legislative priorities from the Ferguson Group. Furthermore, the council approved an excused absence for Mayor Williams and settled the meeting agenda for upcoming sessions.

agenda_items.title: Go Durham Access Paratransit Financial Model & Cost Pressures
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented an overview of the Go Durham Access paratransit system, highlighting increasing ridership, wage growth under labor agreements, and a low 6% county reimbursement rate. Council discussed the growing financial gap and projected out-year deficits ranging from $8 million to nearly $12 million.

agenda_items.title: Go Durham Access Eligibility & Cost Reduction Policy Options
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed potential policy options to mitigate transit fund shortfalls, including restricting Go Durham Access eligibility to the federal 3/4-mile requirement, discontinuing off-duty DPD officer security at Durham Station, cutting the regional call center, eliminating PBGC pension insurance, and reinstating fare collection.

agenda_items.title: Fair-Free Transit Policy & Durham County Transit Plan Funding
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and Council deliberated on the fair-free transit policy, comparing Durham's funding model with Go Raleigh and Wake County. Discussion covered county transit sales tax revenues, financial reserves, and the Board of County Commissioners' decision to decline the city's request for $2.2 million in annual fair-free support.

agenda_items.title: Parking Operations, Garage Usage & CIP Transition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council discussed parking fund finances, utilization of the new downtown parking garage, and potential on-street vs. garage parking incentives. The session concluded with a transition to discuss the Capital Improvement Program (CIP) following a short break.

votes.item_title: Excused absence for Mayor Williams for September 17 meeting
votes.discussion_detail: This routine procedural vote addressed an excused absence for Mayor Williams for the September 17 meeting during the budget retreat discussions. The transcript excerpt focuses on presentations regarding GoDurham Access paratransit system performance and contracting. No debate or dissenting votes occurred on this procedural item.

disagreements.issue: Western Intake Partnership (WIP) withdrawal by partner utilities and long-term infrastructure planning/costs
disagreements.summary: Discussion regarding the Western Intake Partnership after partner utilities opted out of upfront participation, focusing on regionalism, capital costs, water quality, and rate impacts.
disagreements.side_a_position: Expressed concern over the loss of regional partnership while acknowledging the necessity of moving forward with the project for Durham's water security.
side_a_arguments: Council members and city staff noted that the withdrawal of partner utilities is a loss for regionalism and changes cost recovery timelines down the road, making finished water costs primarily Durham's responsibility.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintained that despite partner withdrawal, the project remains the best decision for Durham's long-term water needs and operational efficiency.
side_b_arguments: City staff and management emphasized that upfront capital costs for Durham remain unchanged, and operational savings (such as treating water closer to Durham and utilizing raw water integration) will help offset future cost differences.
disagreements.resolution: Durham City Council received updates and discussed the situation, noting that while partner utilities withdrew from participating upfront, Durham would proceed as the first mover and maintain the raw water intake capacity for future regional use, with operational savings offsetting future costs.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Feb 16, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council convened on February 16, 2026, to discuss community announcements, violent crime rates, homelessness strategies, and budget retreat updates, followed by a public hearing and extensive deliberations on the Lee Village Center mixed-use rezoning and annexation request. After negotiating numerous proffers regarding affordable housing percentages, park land dedication and financial contributions, tree coverage, and pedestrian connectivity, the council unanimously approved the utility extension agreement, zoning ordinance amendments, and consistency statement for the project.

agenda_items.title: Opening, Roll Call, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The meeting opened with a moment of silence, the Pledge of Allegiance, and the roll call. Council members delivered announcements regarding upcoming community events, local meetings, and municipal updates.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Council reviewed and approved the consent agenda, which included routine items, municipal contracts, and project authorizations, with specific items pulled for separate discussion.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed unanimously (exact tally and vote recorded in council records)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: FY 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented the proposed fiscal year 2026-2027 annual action plan for affordable housing and community development needs in Durham neighborhoods, followed by public comments.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing & Consideration: Lee Village Center Annexation & Rezoning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and deliberation on a request for utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation, and initial zoning map change for Lee Village Center across multiple parcels.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed, 5-2 (Councillors Burriss and Cook voting no on annexation/rezoning)

votes.item_title: Utility Extension Agreement with NGR Investment LLC (Lee Village Center)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously after extensive negotiations on proffers.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Council considered a motion to authorize the city manager to enter into a utility extension agreement with NGR Investment LLC for the Lee Village Center project. Discussion leading up to the vote involved commitments regarding pedestrian-oriented design for non-residential buildings, minimum 12-foot sidewalks, commercial use design standards, and a one-time donation of $100,000 to the Durham Parks Foundation alongside at least 2 acres of land dedicated to parks and rec. Additional provisions included a minimum of 10% duplex units, 9,500 square feet of commercial space, AMI terms for townhouse duplexes set at a 30-year tenure, environmentally sensitive open space, and an extra acre of tree coverage. The motion passed unanimously (7-0).

votes.item_title: Ordinance Amending UDO for Lee Village Center Rezoning
votes.notes: Passed unanimously following final proffer adjustments.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Council considered adopting an ordinance amending the unified development ordinance (UDO) to rezone property out of residential suburban 20 (RS-20) and residential suburban multi-family with development plan Falls Jordan Watershed Overlay District B, establishing the same as planned development residential (PDR) with an area of 8.346 acres under the Falls Jordan Watershed Overlay District B. The measure was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously (7-0).

votes.discussion_detail: The City Council considered adopting a consistency statement as required by North Carolina General Statute 160D-605 regarding the Lee Village Center rezoning and development plan. Following a motion and second, the measure passed unanimously (7-0), with the record noting Council Member Baker's participation in development cases during the session.

member_justifications.stance_summary: States she is not weighing the project's substantive merits because she believes the ordinance/statute uses a mandatory 'shall' requiring a TIA before the case reaches City Council rather than deferring TIAs to site plan. Votes no on procedural and statutory grounds.
member_justifications.key_quote: I still believe that the TIA needed to be done prior to it's getting to the council... It is a mandatory shall, not a discretionary on how we feel about when a TIA would be best done.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Argues there are too many unknowns regarding infrastructure capacity, the NC 54 traffic corridor, and the timing of the TIA to support the project as presented. Acknowledges the developer's proffers and generational wealth goals but votes no.
member_justifications.key_quote: There are too many unknowns for me at this moment to support this. I'm really concerned about the infrastructure to continue to grow in Durham and I feel as though I still have concerns about that traffic corridor.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Acknowledges the Planning Commission's concerns and real traffic impacts on neighbors' quality of life, while weighing those against housing needs, 15-minute city transit connectivity, vertical mixed-use, green building, 100-year stormwater, and enhanced buffers. Secures an improved 6% at 60% AMI / 3% at 80% AMI apartment affordability proffer and removal of the transit precondition on park dedication, noting site-plan-level TIAs will help mitigate traffic.
member_justifications.key_quote: I do think that there's a material benefit with the TIA at every stage of site plan where it will come to us to review and accept before it can move forward, which is not something that we have seen with other projects.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports the 20-year townhome deed restriction to allow buyers to build generational wealth and praises the commercial location near I-40. Cites Durham's rapid growth, homelessness recommendations, and 12,000-unit affordable housing gap as reasons why adding diverse housing supply is essential.
member_justifications.key_quote: We have a housing assessment done that talks about the housing diversity that we need... supply meeting that demand also helps out with the cost of it.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Explains that since joining the Planning Commission in 2018 he has fought auto-centric sprawl on Durham's outskirts—noting Durham annexed half the area of Manhattan since 2017 and fell to 97th in park access—and would prefer a Council majority willing to reject large annexations. However, recognizing this Council has elevated expectations, he calls Lee Village Center the best rezoning and annexation case since 2017 due to its design district standards, green building, apartment and townhome affordability, actual greenway construction, and alley-loaded townhomes.
member_justifications.key_quote: This case as it currently sits is the best rezoning and annexation case that I've seen since 2017... I do think that the applicant has brought this case to an elevated standard that we haven't seen.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports keeping the townhome affordability restriction at 20 years rather than extending it to 30 years so working families can build generational wealth through homeownership. Votes in favor of the annexation and rezoning.
member_justifications.key_quote: I want people to come to this country like my family got to come... show up with a suitcase and build their wealth and do better for the next generation.

proffers.environmental_tree: 1 additional acre of tree coverage above UDO minimum; remaining open space located in environmentally sensitive areas; only 1 stream crossing (at Cortez Drive ROW); 100% native plantings for street, vehicular-use, and perimeter buffer trees; Energy Star Multifamily New Construction for all apartments; EV charging stations at apartment amenities
proffers.transit_infrastructure: Bus pullout with shelter along Angier Avenue (subject to GoDurham/GoTriangle); 10-ft shared-use path along east side of Angier Avenue; vehicular/pedestrian connection between Angier Avenue and US 70; turn lanes at driveways on US 70 and Pleasant Drive; traffic signal study at Pleasant and Angier and signal installation if warranted by NCDOT; commercial uses fronting public ROW with minimum 12-ft sidewalks, street trees, and greenway connections
other_proffers: Dedication of at least 2 acres with 100+ linear ft frontage on Angier Avenue for a City public park (or public access easement) plus $100,000 one-time donation to Durham Parks Foundation (increased from $50,000)
Excluded convenience stores with gasoline sales and drive-thru facilities
Minimum 15% rear-loaded alley-accessed townhomes, 15 surface-parked garage-free townhomes, minimum 20% townhomes 1,700 sq ft or less, and 45-ft building height limit on western portion

member_justifications.stance_summary: Commends the applicant for returning after an earlier denial with Angier-to-US 70 connectivity, attainable high-$200k target townhome pricing, transit-corridor infill, strong park and school proffers, and 5-6% blended affordability. Secures commitments for a minimum 10% duplex mix and a minimum 9,500 sq ft commercial component, noting Durham needs housing supply to stabilize rents.
member_justifications.key_quote: I really appreciate you coming back with an improved project addressing some of these connectivity things... I think this is a great project. I'm happy to support.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Pushes for and secures an expansion of for-sale income-restricted units from 3% at 80% AMI to 5% (adding 2% at 100% AMI and covering duplexes) and doubles the earmarked Durham Parks Foundation contribution from $50,000 to $100,000. Praises the applicant's intentional traffic work and well-thought-out infill design.
member_justifications.key_quote: I do appreciate y'all coming back with what appears to me to be a really well-thought-out project that really meets the needs of this area.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Acknowledges resident traffic crash maps on US 70 while noting the Angier-to-US 70 connection and TPO boulevard plans should help channel traffic, and secures commitments to place remaining open space in environmentally sensitive areas and add 1 acre of tree coverage above UDO minimums. Highlights the balance of ecological protection, parks, infill housing, and diverse price points.
member_justifications.key_quote: I do really like this as an infill project. I appreciate the park's commitments that you've come forward with, especially with the enhanced proffers this evening.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Notes he proudly voted against the prior Cortez rezoning on the eastern parcel two years earlier and checks with planning staff to verify that 8% affordable apartments across up to 630 units will not yield fewer affordable units than the legacy 10% on 350 units. Secures a proffer requiring commercial buildings to front public rights-of-way with minimum 12-ft sidewalks, street trees, and greenway connections, and votes aye.
member_justifications.key_quote: This case was 2 years ago. It was the Cortez rezoning case... Just want to make sure I'm understanding and that we're not losing potential affordable units.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Thanks the applicant for generous affordable housing commitments while wishing more units could be delivered holistically rather than piecemeal and expressing concern about existing traffic congestion before long-term TPO fixes arrive. Also challenges the assumption that building more market-rate apartments alone prevents renter displacement or junk fees, though she joins the unanimous approval.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Friday, February 13, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held its budget retreat and public hearings for the fiscal year 2026-27 budget and capital improvement plan, reviewing financial projections, maintaining a proposed property tax rate of 43.71 cents, and hearing extensive public comment regarding affordable housing, eviction diversion funding, immigration legal services, community safety, violence reduction, and environmental justice cleanup.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order & Opening Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor and council members opened the budget retreat meeting with roll call and opening remarks welcoming attendees to the Durham County facility. City manager and budget staff outlined the scope of the two-day budget retreats focused on aligning the budget with the strategic plan refresh.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Budget Retreat Kickoff & Strategic Priorities
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City manager delivered the budget retreat opening address, setting the tone for the upcoming budget process. The address emphasized balancing ongoing commitments with new priorities using a chess and jigsaw metaphor for sequencing municipal investments.

agenda_items.title: Financial Update & Budget Outlook
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and management services presented financial projections and a fiscal outlook for the city. Staff reviewed property tax trends, the recent revaluation impacts from the prior year, and expected revenues for the upcoming fiscal year.

agenda_items.title: Staff Compensation & Livable Wage Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Human resources staff presented compensation updates, focusing on staff retention, salary structures, and the impact of the Durham Minimum Livable Wage policy on the city's personnel budget.

agenda_items.title: Transit Operations & Capital Improvements Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented updates on transit operations, including funding requirements for the zero-fare transit program, capital projects, and maintaining transit infrastructure under growing cost pressures.

agenda_items.title: Resident Satisfaction Survey Results
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented the results of the resident satisfaction survey, providing statistically valid feedback from across Durham on municipal service delivery, community priorities, and quality of life indicators.

agenda_items.title: Community Conversations & Housing Stability Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and council discussed community conversation findings regarding housing and neighborhood stability, rental pressures, displacement risks, and affordable housing needs across Durham.

votes.item_title: FY 2026-27 Budget Public Hearings & Strategic Plan Discussion
votes.discussion_detail: The meeting opened with a roll call by city leadership, confirming the presence of Council members Nate Baker, Shanetta Burr, Chelsea Cook, Matt Kovac, and Crist, alongside the city manager, attorney, and clerk. Director Christina Rearen of the budget and management services department welcomed council members to the first of two budget retreats held on Friday the 13th, providing housekeeping details regarding facilities. Director Rearen outlined that the primary focus of the session was a strategic plan refresh designed to directly drive the upcoming fiscal year budget over the two-day retreat.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Friday, February 13, 2026
disagreements.issue: Eviction Diversion and Legal Aid Funding vs Landlord Impacts
disagreements.summary: Debate between housing advocates supporting eviction diversion/legal aid funding and landlords/housing providers concerned about financial impacts and housing supply reductions.
disagreements.side_a_position: Pro-Funding / Tenant Protection
side_a_arguments: Legal aid and eviction diversion programs are essential anti-displacement tools that prevent homelessness, protect vulnerable tenants, and hold landlords accountable.
disagreements.side_b_position: Critical of Legal Aid Funding / Landlord Perspective
side_b_arguments: Extensive legal aid involvement and delay tactics increase financial hardship for housing providers/landlords, reduce affordable housing supply, and can lead to property sales rather than continued affordable rentals.
side_b_members: David Mafully and other housing providers
disagreements.resolution: Public comments and council discussions addressed the tension between funding legal aid for eviction diversion versus landlord financial impacts and housing supply, with the manager's proposed budget maintaining the prior year's commitment.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Feb 5, 2026 (full meeting)
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held its work session on February 5, 2026, chaired by Mayor Pro Tem Javiera Caballero in the absence of Mayor Williams. The council discussed and received annual reports from various boards and commissions, reviewed priority items including a capital improvement contract for radio tower site additions and relocation with Motorola Solutions, and engaged in an in-depth discussion with planning staff regarding riparian buffer protection standards and No Practical Alternatives (NPA) authorizations. The council also approved excused absences for upcoming meetings and officially settled the meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call & Council Member Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Opening roll call was held noting Mayor Williams excused. Council members shared announcements regarding city workers during winter weather, board and commission annual reports, Black History Month events, white flag shelter extensions, and transit equity day.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items & Introductions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager highlighted priority agenda item 6 regarding radio tower site additions due to expiring bids and introduced new Human Resources Director Aaron Miley while recognizing outgoing acting HR director Montique.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences for Council Members Burris and Copek
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members requested and were granted excused absences for the upcoming February 19, 2026 work session.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments & Citizen Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public comments were delivered regarding public tennis court maintenance and USA tennis programming opportunities in Durham, as well as water quality advocacy by Sound Rivers.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Pulls & Radio Tower Contract Authorization (Project CB032)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed pulled consent items, suspended rules for agenda item 6, authorized a contract with Motorola Solutions, Inc. for Project CB032 not to exceed $7,716,771.30, and adopted budget ordinance No. 1655 amending the FY 2025-2026 budget.

agenda_items.title: Riparian Buffer Protection Standards Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning and development staff presented an overview of riparian buffer protection standards, No Practical Alternatives Authorizations (NPA), mitigation options, and variance procedures, followed by extensive council Q&A and public comments.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Settlement and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager reviewed finalized consent items, pulled items, and upcoming public hearings (including adding the Creekside zoning case for Feb 19 as item 29), and council voted to settle the agenda before adjourning.

votes.item_title: Excused absence for Council Member Burrus on February 19, 2026
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Shanetta Burris requested an excused absence for the upcoming council meeting on February 19, 2026. A motion was offered by Council Member Matt Kopac and seconded by Council Member Carl Rist, and the request was approved unanimously by the council.

votes.item_title: Excused absence for Council Member Copek on February 19, 2026
votes.discussion_detail: Following the earlier excused absence approval, Council Member Matt Kopac requested an excused absence for the same date of February 19, 2026. A motion was made by Council Member Cook and seconded by Council Member Baker, and the request carried unanimously.

votes.item_title: Suspend the rules for Agenda Item 6 (Radio tower site additions and relocation with Motorola Solutions, Inc.)
votes.discussion_detail: To accommodate business regarding Agenda Item 6 concerning radio tower site additions and relocation with Motorola Solutions, Inc., a motion to suspend the rules and vote was introduced. The motion was moved by Council Member Baker and seconded by Council Member Carl Rist, and successfully passed with unanimous support.

votes.item_title: Authorize contract with Motorola Solutions, Inc. for Project CB032 not to exceed $7,716,71.30
votes.discussion_detail: The council considered authorizing the city manager to negotiate and execute a contract with Motorola Solutions, Inc. to complete capital improvement project CB032 in an amount not to exceed $7,716,71.30. The motion was moved by Council Member Baker and seconded by Council Member Cook, passing unanimously without any recorded opposition.

votes.item_title: Adopt budget ordinance amending FY 2025-2026 budget (Ordinance No. 1655) for radio tower project CB032
votes.discussion_detail: As a companion measure to the Motorola Solutions contract for capital improvement project CB032, a motion was presented to adopt a budget ordinance amending the FY 2025-2026 city budget, designated as Ordinance Number 1655, for the purpose of adding additional funding to the project. The motion was moved by Council Member Baker and seconded by Council Member Carl Rist, and passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Settle the meeting agenda
votes.discussion_detail: Following a rich discussion covering developer proffer details, stringent stream regulations, and the impacts on regular homeowners versus large developers, the City Manager presented the proposed meeting agenda. The agenda included consent items 1 through 5 and 7 through 24, GBA public hearings items 26 and 27, and the addition of item 29 (the creekside item). Council Member Carl Rist moved to settle the agenda, seconded by Council Member Cook, and the motion carried unanimously before the meeting adjourned at 3:10 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting February 2, 2026 (Virtual)
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held a virtual meeting on February 2, 2026, due to winter weather conditions. The council unanimously voted to refer a controversial contract with Peregrine Technologies for a police operations management platform back to staff. They also approved the manager's priority items, several consent agenda items, appointments to the Durham Performing Arts Center oversight committee, and adopted a substitute motion for the Curly Gardens annexation/utility extension allowing city water service to be extended to the property without full annexation.

agenda_items.title: Opening, Roll Call & Virtual Meeting Housekeeping
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams called the virtual meeting to order at 7:00 PM, followed by a moment of silence and the Pledge of Allegiance. City Clerk conducted the roll call, and the Mayor outlined housekeeping rules for the virtual Zoom webinar format.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Announcements & Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members shared announcements, recognizing Black History Month, local frontline workers, sanitation crews, and winter storm recovery efforts. Council Member Rist highlighted Transit Equity Day and local tax assistance programs.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Ferguson presented priority items, recommending referring the Peregrine Technologies police operations platform contract back to staff and granting a continuance for the Creek Side mixed-use development zoning map change.

agenda_items.title: Refer Peregrine Technologies Contract Back to Staff
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Council considered the Manager's priority item to refer the controversial Peregrine Technologies contract back to staff without further consideration, following extensive community feedback. Council members expressed support for the manager's recommendation.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed, 7-0 (Motion by Rist, Second by Cabayro, unanimous roll call vote).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Items 1, 2, 5, and 9 pulled)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Council reviewed and approved the consent agenda, noting that items 1, 2, 5, and 9 were pulled for separate public comment or discussion.

agenda_items.title: Infrastructure Contracts & Paving Projects Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearings and presentations were held for capital infrastructure contracts including street repairs, paving, and stormwater projects (Items 4 and 5). Public commenters raised equity concerns regarding capital investments in historically underserved neighborhoods like Hayti compared to gentrifying areas.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation - Curly Gardens & Utility Extension
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and extensive deliberation on the consolidated annexation for Curly Gardens (Item 17). Property owners and representatives requested water line extension and annexation for 36 multi-family affordable housing units, while community members raised transparency concerns regarding future expansion into Orange County and urban growth boundary (UGB) implications. Ultimately, Council opted for a substitute motion to authorize a utility extension agreement without full annexation.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed substitute motion 6-0 authorizing utility extension agreement without full annexation.

agenda_items.title: DPAC Oversight Committee & Board Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Council voted on board and committee appointments, including the Mayor's Council for Women and the Durham Performing Arts Center (DPAC) Oversight Committee appointments.

votes.item_title: Manager's Priority Item: Refer Peregrine Technologies contract back to staff
votes.discussion_detail: This manager's priority item involved referring the Peregrine Technologies contract back to staff following public feedback and review. Council members expressed appreciation for the manager's wisdom in referring the item back and for staff listening to council sentiments. Moved by Council Member Carl Rist and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Javiera Caballero, the motion passed unanimously 7-0 on a voice vote.

votes.item_title: Substitute Motion for Curly Gardens: Authorize City Manager to enter into utility extension agreement without full annexation
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered an infill project case for Curly Gardens, where Council Member Cook proposed solely extending utilities rather than pursuing full annexation. Council Member Carl Rist agreed with the approach as a sound infill project with no traffic concerns, while staff provided context on policies and cost-benefit analysis. A substitute motion was framed by the city attorney and planning director to authorize the city manager to enter into a utility extension agreement with the Sidu Living Trust Trustee. Moved by Council Member Cook, the substitute motion passed unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: DPAC Oversight Committee Appointments (Rems and James Bullock)
votes.discussion_detail: The mayor brought forward committee appointments for the Durham Performing Arts Center oversight committee. The motion proposed appointing Rems representing arts and culture and James Bullock representing facility management, with terms expiring on March 1st, 2029. Properly moved and seconded, the appointments passed unanimously 6-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 2, 2026 (Virtual)
disagreements.issue: Curly Gardens Annexation vs Utility Extension
disagreements.summary: Discussion over whether to approve annexation for Curly Gardens Apartments or limit action to a utility extension agreement.
disagreements.side_a_position: Favor annexation and city water connection for the 36-unit affordable housing parcel.
side_a_arguments: Applicant and property owners (Bergman family / Curly Gardens Apartments) requested annexation to secure city water and replace an aging community well, citing maintenance costs and reliability concerns.
disagreements.side_b_position: Opposed full annexation to prevent UGB expansion, advocating instead for a limited utility extension agreement that provides water without annexing the parcel into the city.
side_b_arguments: Residents and public commenters raised concerns that annexation would crack the urban growth boundary (UGB) and serve as a stepping stone for a planned 84-unit expansion into Orange County.
disagreements.resolution: Adopted a substitute motion (6-0) to approve only the utility extension agreement rather than full annexation, avoiding expansion of the urban growth boundary (UGB) while granting water access.

development_cases.location: Research Triangle Park (existing RTP boundaries outside city limits)
development_cases.scale: Text amendment creating new UC-3 zoning district across Articles 4, 5, 6, and 7 (no city properties affected)
